entries.text: Drugs map: body effects (beta) as a third input, so drugs can be placed by the effects their receptors may produce (inferred from the sourced receptor effects and each binding's direction, weighted by the strongest affinity), alone or with receptors and neurotransmitter tone. New "Antipsychotics: body effects" preset.

Drugs map: the inputs are now toggles combinable freely instead of a receptors / tone / both switch, "net tone" is renamed neurotransmitter tone, and the plot title gets one clause per input. Old links with both still open.
Drugs map: the plot title names a class in the plural ("Antihistamines", "MAO inhibitors") and a target by its short name ("MAO-A" rather than "Monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A)")
Drugs map: five more presets, antihistamines by H1 vs M1, psychedelics on the serotonin receptors, MAOIs by MAO-A vs MAO-B, opioids on mu / kappa / delta, stimulants by DAT vs NET

Drugs map: a Presets box loads a ready-made view in one click (antipsychotics by dopamine receptors, D2 vs 5-HT2A, side-effect receptors, antidepressants by SERT vs NET or by profile, sleep and anxiety drugs, every drug by transmitter tone)
Drugs map: the drug nearest the pointer always shows its name, even when it was hidden by another; on a phone the first tap shows and highlights it, a second tap opens it
Drugs map: a title over the plot says what is on screen, and the default zoom backs off so it never hides a point
Drugs map README: one folded picture per preset, a table of contents, and the hosting notes folded away
Drugs map: a search box at the top of the class filter and of the axes picker finds a class or a target by typing (accents, case and dashes ignored, so "5ht2a" finds 5-HT2A)
Drugs map: the title is centred and shortened to "Drugs map", and the introduction uses the full page width

The drugs map READMEs link the terms they use (principal component analysis, affinity, agonist, NbN, PDSP, Guide to Pharmacology...) to their Wikipedia article in the README’s language, or to the official site
The drugs map README opens with what the map does, then an example picture in the README’s own language; the French README is titled DrugsMap
The drugs map’s loading spinner could stay on screen over a finished map after quick successive changes (resizing, fast filter clicks)
The drugs map README opens with a picture of the map that links to the same live view

The drugs map places drugs by measured affinities only: drugs with no measured Ki are no longer shown, and a new “Measured Ki only” switch (on by default) leaves out bindings without one instead of guessing their strength. “Filter by” is now “Filter points by” and comes before “Color by”
In the README, the drugs map links to its own README, with the live site in parentheses
The drugs map page opens with a short pitch linking to neurarium, and its README opens on GitHub, in your language, instead of as raw text
With “See inside” on, hovering names the solid structure under the cursor instead of the see-through lobe in front of it, matching what a click selects

The drugs map is now a page of its own, opened in a new tab from the Drugs list (also at drugsmap.olicorne.org): it loads much faster since it skips the 3D brain, and clicking a drug opens it in the 3D atlas. Old links to the map still work
The drugs map has its own README (English and French), and the About popup's data section, the README and llms.txt cite it as an example of what neurarium's open data files allow
Swipe the panel’s title bar to resize it: up grows it (folded, half screen, full screen), down shrinks it; a tap still folds or unfolds it
Moving the mouse over the brain no longer slows its rotation: the structure under the cursor is looked up at most 20 times a second instead of on every mouse move
The brain starts centred in the space beside the panel and stays centred as it auto-rotates, instead of drifting right and low (it turned about a point centred for the first angle only)
The drug map is renamed the drugs map, and opens on currently marketed drugs only (untick it in Advanced to see every drug)
Drugs with identical binding profiles (the benzodiazepines) no longer pile into one illegible lump on the drugs map: they unfold into a spiral spaced a dot apart
The drug map can be rotated with a two-finger twist (or shift-scroll), and touching dots are spread apart by at most one dot width, with a faint line back to their true place
The drug map's class filter groups the classes into families (antidepressants, antipsychotics, stimulants...), each selectable as a whole
The drug map's controls sit in rounded boxes folded by default (Inputs with its type and axes, Color by, Filter by, Advanced), and its legend and axis meaning in folded boxes under the plot
Drug map dots slide to their new place when the view changes, and fade in or out when they appear or leave; a spinner shows while a slow device recomputes, with a hint to reload past 5 seconds
The drug map carries an author byline under its title, and its watermark carries the app version

The drug map picks its input targets from a list grouped by transmitter system: click a system to take it whole or a target to take it alone, shift-click or long-press drops, with All and None buttons
The drug map's title carries a beta tag, and a drug's name opens (or hides) it like its dot

Drug map pan and pinch: a finger landing on a dot can pan or pinch, lifting one finger of a pinch keeps panning, a lost pointer no longer turns the next touch into a pinch, and a gesture never opens or hides a drug

The drug map button is bigger, reads "Show on a map" and carries a beta tag; the map has a grey plot well with a grid at one scale for both axes, pinch zoom, names sized to how crowded the points are and never overlapping, a folded class list and legend, shift-click (long-press) to drop one class, and nomenclature colours matched to class colours

The drug map controls sit in labelled rows (input coordinates, colour, filters, then a folded Advanced with names, normalization and signs all on by default), with a fullscreen button and a "currently marketed only" filter; the approval-year inputs are gone, a decade link still sets a range shown as a removable chip
One spelling per Neuroscience-based Nomenclature label: SN-RI, DN-RIRe, Glu-CB and Glu were each written two ways, now guarded by a test

A Drug map button atop the Drugs list (and a "map" link on each list heading) opens a 2D map of every drug placed by a PCA of its binding profile, recomputed for the drugs on screen, with class chips, an approval-year range, hidden drugs, names, normalization and colouring by class, nomenclature, year or lab, all kept in the URL

The drug map can plot chosen targets directly (for example 5-HT2A against D2), count agonists and antagonists with opposite signs, place drugs by net neurotransmission or by receptors and net tone together, and colour drugs by major metabolic route or by Ki coverage; clicking a drug opens it in a new tab
The Drugs list can be sorted by class, name, first approval decade or half-life, with each row showing its year or half-life, and the filter box now also matches an approval year

Active metabolites gain 11 measured Ki values (norclozapine at D2, D3, M1, M2, M4 and delta-opioid; norquetiapine at 5-HT2B; levoamphetamine at DAT and NET; levomethamphetamine at NET; norketamine at NMDA) and 54 newly found PDSP binding sites, so their predicted effects sort by affinity instead of falling last
A drug's Predicted effects can be grouped by effect or by receptor with a switch at the top of the section, and the choice is remembered
Predicted effects say "could cause" once at the top instead of on every row, and are ordered by the drug's Ki (tightest binding first, unmeasured last), each receptor showing its Ki

Every panel section now always appears, even when empty: an empty one says "No information about ... for this receptor yet", so a panel shows what the dataset tracks elsewhere (e.g. age and sex differences on 5-HT3)
The About popup now says a text-only version exists for LLMs and links llms.txt and /api/
Each section of an /api text page is also served alone, e.g. /api/drug/sertraline/bindings, so an LLM reads only what it needs
The /api text pages now use exactly the panel's headings, subtitles, labels and notes, read from the same strings, and a test fails whenever the panels and the text version drift apart
In the /api text pages each claim carries its sources on its own line, a grades legend heads every page, and a claim written by an LLM from memory is spelled out as UNSOURCED
Clinical section names and plain-language subtitles across the receptor, structure, connection, circuit, group, effect and enzyme panels; "Found in" becomes "Regional distribution"
Plainer explanations for psychiatrists across hints, notes, the Sources popup and the tour
Source links in some tooltips (enzyme roles, doubted claims, median Ki) showed as plain text instead of a clickable link
The pathway symmetry note now says plainly that left/right symmetry is assumed
The guided tour frames the structure illustration again
The pre-push hook also runs the JavaScript tests
A receptor's Effects section now groups its effects under Agonism, Antagonism and the other modes, instead of naming the mode on every row
A fast test now checks that every guided-tour step still points at something the app has, and that its text exists in English and French

Drug panel sections now use clinical names (Identification, Pharmacokinetics, Pharmacodynamics, Metabolism, Monitoring...), each with a short plain-language subtitle that stays visible while the section is folded
A new Pharmacogenomics section groups the CPIC dosing advice and the ClinPGx gene-variant associations
The headless tour check follows the highlight ring's destination, so it no longer stalls on a slow machine
Direct molecular targets now lists the active metabolites' own bindings among the drug's, each row naming its compound, under a warning that several compounds contribute
Psychotropic interactions is now a subsection of Metabolism, and every beta section sits at the bottom of the drug panel
"Inferred side effects" is renamed "Inferred effects", and Genetic variability carries the beta label

The drug panel's "Acts within" section is folded into Neurotransmitter tone: a system the drug reaches only through a postsynaptic receptor is now a "no tone change" row there, with one line saying why
Every data-sourcing step can be re-run without undoing another step's work, every saved cache has one fixed format, and tests check both
Seven more verified drug classes: bumetanide, cannabidiol, cannabinol, furosemide, nabilone, rimonabant and tiapride
Three more sourced pathways: raphe to caudate, raphe to putamen, and frontal cortex to putamen

Six more active-metabolite bindings: noribogaine at the serotonin transporter and the kappa and mu opioid receptors, norzimelidine at the serotonin and noradrenaline transporters, 2-oxoquazepam at the alpha7 nicotinic receptor
Measured affinities for benztropine at the dopamine transporter, naltrexone at the delta and kappa opioid receptors and fentanyl at kappa, plus benztropine at 5-HT2A
Five receptor-effect caveats are now judged like every other quote
The server image builds again: the agent-facing /api pages renderer was missing two shared helpers, and a test now replays that build step locally

Six drugs (diazepam, diphenhydramine, lorazepam, mirtazapine, olanzapine, sildenafil) no longer list a brand literally named "Other", and a placeholder name can no longer enter as a brand, holder or originator
Re-running the binding-direction table and metabolite fetchers offline reproduces their saved results again, and a test now checks the fetchers against their committed caches
The sourcing gaps document now lists only the gaps that are open today, with its figures generated from the data and a test keeping dates and stale counts out
Every source page is read through one shared reader, and the non-receptor target filter exists once
The Data browser now lists the gene-based dosing rows and the genetic-variant rows, and a test checks every kind's rows against the coverage tally
Opening a link with only a language or tour setting no longer stops the brain from spinning; only a link that frames a specific view does

Less duplicated code in the data tools: one gene map, one grade ranking, one Ki-quote check, one page reader and quote gate for every sourcing pass, one hemisphere-suffix rule, and unused imports removed, with no change to the published data

The drug panel is reorganised: class and nomenclature sit in Administrative, brain entry is a Pharmacokinetics subsection, active metabolites open the Metabolism section, and the genetics-driven dosing advice moves inside Metabolism as "Genetics-caused posology adaptation"
Clearer section names: "Genetic variability", "Psychotropic interactions" (which now says only drugs present in Neurarium are compared) and "Inferred side effects"
Brands are shown on one alphabetically sorted row
A newly opened panel starts with its sections folded, while each open tab keeps the sections you unfolded

The neurotransmitter tone, inferred side effects and release changes of a drug now include its active metabolites, each contribution labelled by compound, under a warning that several compounds contribute

Leftover expression sources for receptor groups that were split long ago are pruned, and the data check now re-verifies every stored quote of every corpus against its page, so an orphaned quote can no longer hide
The README sourcing figures are up to date again, and one test now fails whenever any committed generated file falls behind its generator
Every data tool refuses a page name shaped like a file path, enforced by a lint test

Developer docs point at where the code lives after the restructure, the tools runbook gets a table of contents and one heading per sourcing pass, and a test now fails if a source corpus goes undocumented
The quote recheck tool reads uncertainty reasons containing quotation marks in English again instead of falling back to French

Viewer restructure: data loading, translations, startup, guided tour, data browser, search and the drug interactions section each split into small focused files, with one shared helper for grades, network fetches, link parameters and scene focus; nothing changes on screen

Data tooling restructure: shared helpers move out of individual scripts into one library folder, the data check is split into one small module per check family, and the data generator is split into small build stages with its corpus list and statistics in their own files; the published data is unchanged

Data tooling cleanup: one list of node kinds and one "backed" count shared by the generator, the data check and the README stats, and more sourcing passes check their quotes through the shared page gate
A shared simulation link with an absurd dose ratio no longer breaks every curve: the ratio is kept between 0.1 and 100
A bad ghost-opacity value in a view link is ignored instead of making the brain invisible
Clicking quickly between structures no longer fetches the same Wikipedia summary or changelog twice
The offline cache no longer grows with every language or tour link opened
Guided-tour text is escaped before display, closing a latent injection path
Viewer cleanup: one helper for external links and buttons, no more state hidden on page elements, dead translation fallbacks and an unused export removed
The data tool that lists drug bindings still missing a source runs again: it crashed on a binding measured without a known direction
When the server answers with an error, the app now keeps showing the copy it already had instead of the error page
Opening "What's new" while offline no longer marks the unread notes as read
Every link taken from the data, including the ClinPGx variant link, now has to be a web address before it is shown
Clean-up of the code behind the panels: one shared builder for page elements, one shared "Found in" section for receptors and targets, and every saved preference read in one place
The data tools write their files atomically, refuse a citation page that looks like a file path, and share one reader for the Stahl index, the quote check and the judged files
The site image builds again: a file the agent pages need was left out of the build
A doubted holder, originator, physchem value or NbN class now shows its orange "uncertain" pill instead of a green one
The Effects section hides itself when its index cannot be loaded, instead of showing an empty list
The new-version check retries later when a reload still lands on the old build, and never reloads under an open guided tour
Opening another panel closes a pinned tooltip; the dev banner is built without innerHTML
A PDSP measurement cited by an uncertainty reason now reads in full in its tooltip (row, Ki, species, radioligand, paper) instead of a bare database name
MDMA's 5-HT1B and 5-HT1D partial agonism is marked contradicted: two human receptor screens found MDMA inactive at both up to 10000 nM
GtoPdb function rows are offered for receptor effects only when human, as documented; an isolated-tissue flag cites every isolated-tissue source
Every model-picked quote now carries a fingerprint of its sentence, so a rebuilt worklist can never attach a verdict to a different sentence
The data checks gate more: one walk for grades and quotes, measured Ki rows behind uncertainty reasons, node ids, and every viewer module for unbound names
The viewer's code is split from one 10 500-line file into focused modules, and its styles move out of the page into stylesheets; nothing on screen changes
The sourcing tools share one HTTP helper, one quote gate, one cache loader and one salt-word list instead of copies, and the EMA fetcher only follows EMA links

39 more bindings stated in the Wikipedia articles of Stahl drugs (clomipramine, memantine, viloxazine, naltrexone, aripiprazole VMAT2, ...), added only where Stahl lists no binding on that target, each quote checked
Dimenhydrinate is now shown as a salt of diphenhydramine and 8-chlorotheophylline and borrows diphenhydramine's bindings, each tagged so
Salvinorin A's D2 partial agonism is marked contradicted by a 50-receptor screen, and 12 new bindings the article itself hedges are marked speculative
Stahl drugs may now carry a Wikipedia binding on a target Stahl does not list; Stahl's own bindings are never overwritten
Every receptor's Effects section now shows something: a sourced effect, or a blue "unknown" pill saying which sources were searched and when; 5-HT1F gains antimigraine and sedation from papers

Eight new effects (bronchoconstriction, more gastric acid, muscle weakness, exaggerated startle, night blindness, ataxia, itch, itch relief), so glycine, mGluR1, mGluR6 and the muscle nicotinic receptor now have sourced effects
An effect backed only by isolated human tissue (not living patients) now carries an orange warning

Workup: checks the label asks only for some patients now show as "only if: ...", quoting the label; every label line was judged, and drugs with no French product use their European (EMA) label, so 246 checks over 85 drugs
33 new drug bindings stated in the drugs' Wikipedia articles (amantadine, isoflurane, nitrous oxide, methamphetamine, ...), each quote checked
A tab showing an older build (a restored tab, or an offline launch) now reloads onto the latest version as soon as the server answers
Any data point can now be marked contradicted; amisulpride's tentative D2 partial agonism is flagged against GtoPdb, Wikipedia and a cAMP assay
The effects index is computed once at build time instead of twice
"GABA-A-rho" no longer matches every GABA-A sentence when mining prose
UNKNOWN effects, the tissue flag, site-keyed contradictions, the binding-gap pass and the EMA label fallback are documented

BETA: a new Effects section lists every clinical effect (nausea, sedation, weight gain, ...); opening one shows the receptors that carry it, each with its source, and the drugs that could cause it through their bindings, searchable in English and French and linkable
For AI agents: llms.txt and the /api/ pages now carry the effect to receptors to drugs index, one page per effect
The Effects section and its agent twin are documented

BETA: a drug panel now lists the checks its French label (RCP sections 4.2 to 4.4) asks for, before starting and during treatment (ECG, blood count, liver tests, weight, drug level, ...), each quoted from the label and linked to the official BDPM page; 146 checks over 52 drugs, not medical advice
The BDPM section reader is split so the label's other sections can be read with the same code

Receptor effects gain a second source, the IUPHAR/BPS Guide to Pharmacology's curated function and pathophysiology notes (human data only): 164 sourced effects, now including beta3 bladder relaxation, M5 vasodilation and 5-HT4 gut motility

A drug panel now has a "Brain entry" section: how fat-soluble the drug is (XLogP3) and how polar (polar surface area), computed by PubChem, plus whether it crosses the blood-brain barrier (BBB+ or BBB-, with logBB when measured) from the B3DB dataset, each with a tooltip on how to read it

The drug panel's Administrative section now names who invented the drug (with the company's current name when it was bought or renamed, e.g. "Ciba (now Novartis)") and that company's country, both sourced from Wikipedia, for 113 drugs
It also shows the current holder of the marketing authorisation in the United States (Drugs@FDA) and in France (BDPM)
The Sources popup no longer fails to open when an example drug lacks the field it illustrates
A drug panel now has an Administrative section gathering its first approval (with how many years ago, e.g. "1997 (29 years ago)"), any market withdrawals and its brand names
Every source in a tooltip is now a clickable link: the exact Wikipedia revision checked, a paper's DOI, a Drugs@FDA application page, or a book's DOI (ISBN on WorldCat when the book has none)
Haloperidol now carries a sourced note that the brain clears it far more slowly than the blood (brain-tissue half-life of 6.8 days, Kornhuber 1999)

Receptor effects grow from 66 to 151 sourced claims, adding therapeutic effects such as antiemetic, anxiolytic, antipsychotic or sleep promotion, so a drug's panel now shows them too (vortioxetine's 5-HT3 blockade gives an antiemetic effect)
A drug's Neurotransmitter tone rows now show an up or down arrow (tone rises or falls) instead of a left/right one, with a matching tooltip
In a source tooltip, a blank line now separates the quote from "How this quote got here"
The address bar no longer carries auto-rotate, animation or animation-speed settings: a shared link still applies them if present, but never writes them
The Pharmacokinetics values (time to peak, half-life, therapeutic range, alert level) no longer sit glued to the previous value's source badge
The data check no longer flags a quoted drug class label ("Stimulant") as possibly too short
A link opened in the automated screenshot mode no longer leaves the brain blown apart
The data check no longer flags every quoted Ki table row as possibly too short, so the warnings that matter stand out
"See inside" now turns the near lobes to glass instead of making them vanish, fading smoothly as you turn the brain, and a click goes through them to the structure behind
The French notice about AI assistants now reads "Utilisable par les IA"
On a wide screen the brain opened far too small: it now fills the space beside the panel from the start, and Reset brings back that same view
Reset now also puts every 3D setting (Separate, Transparency, Auto-rotate, names, projections, See inside, animations and their speed, arrow colours) back to its default
No more browser warning about the deprecated apple-mobile-web-app-capable tag

The /api text pages now give each source the same link its tooltip in the viewer offers (label page, paper, permalink), use shorter addresses without .md, and say plainly that the 3D version shows slightly more
The README explains why neurarium follows the llms.txt convention rather than running an MCP server

neurarium is AI-ready: the loading screen and the README explain how to paste one link into Claude, ChatGPT, Le Chat or Gemini so the assistant can look up and check any fact here against its quoted source
A mistyped /api address now shows the list of every page with its id instead of a bare error, each kind has its own list (e.g. /api/drug/), and the .md ending is optional

The whole dataset can be read as plain text at /api/: one Markdown page per drug, receptor, region, pathway and circuit, each claim with its grade and the verbatim source quotes listed at the end, for AI assistants and devices that cannot run the 3D viewer
status.json rounds the server's last restart down to 5 minutes

An llms.txt page tells AI assistants where the open dataset lives, what each file holds and how to read a claim's source, and a status.json gives the running version and when the server last restarted

A drug's neurotransmitter tone no longer gives every weak binding a minimum weight: an affinity of 1 µM now adds nothing, so a few weak hits can add up but no longer outweigh one strong block, and an autoreceptor counts half as much as a reuptake block since it only partly brakes release

A drug's "Projections affected" section is now "Neurotransmitter tone (indicative)": each system shows its signed value and, below it, the sum it comes from, one line per binding (target, why it changes the tone, +1 or −1 times its affinity weight, its own source badge), under a warning that this is a rough indicative value and not a clinical measure. A system's list of drugs now shows each drug's tone and is ranked by it
The drug's target list is now called "Direct molecular targets", since it holds transporters and enzymes as well as receptors
Sections you unfold in a panel stay unfolded on the next panel of the same kind, so switching from one drug to another keeps the same sections open for comparison
An uncertain badge's tooltip no longer prints the same database reference twice (once without its link)

A drug's "Acts on" section is now called "Direct action on receptors", and for a drug with active metabolites it opens with a warning naming them, since their own actions are not in that list, with a link that jumps to the Active metabolites section

A source that is not a book now says what its reference is (PubMed id, DailyMed set id, gene, GtoPdb target...) instead of a page number such as "p. 7827213", and links to the record when it has a public page, for example a study's Europe PMC entry
In a drug's Pharmacokinetics formulations, a value's source badge no longer sits almost against the next label

Receptor, target, enzyme, brain structure, circuit and projection group panels now open with their sections folded, like the drug panel: the title, description and key facts stay visible, a heading opens its section, and a jump into a section opens it first

Receptor and target panels gain a "Genetic variants" section: the variants of the receptor's gene that ClinPGx (formerly PharmGKB) associates with how people respond to a drug, grouped by variant (DRD2 Taq1A, OPRM1 A118G, the serotonin transporter's long and short forms, ...), each with its evidence level, a conditional "may be associated with" sentence, the phenotypes, a link to ClinPGx and a source pill carrying ClinPGx's own per-genotype sentences, under one not-medical-advice caveat
A drug panel lists the gene variants ClinPGx annotates for that drug by name, grouped under the receptor or target whose gene carries them

New source: ClinPGx clinical annotations (CC BY-SA 4.0), 546 annotations over 46 receptor and target genes at evidence levels 1A to 3 (level 4 left out; all but two are level 3, a single study or several that do not clearly agree), each quote copied verbatim from a committed, pinned export and re-checked against it on every build

Olanzapine + Samidorphan's two active metabolites now carry an orange "contradicted" pill: Stahl lists N-dealkylated samidorphan and samidorphan N-oxide as acting on the mu opioid receptor, while the US Lybalvi label states "Neither metabolite contributes to the pharmacological effects of samidorphan". Both are kept and the label sentence is quoted in the pill's tooltip

Receptor and target panels gain an "Across age and sex" section (beta): what human PET and SPECT studies report about how much of a receptor or transporter the brain carries as people age or between women and men (D2, D1, dopamine and serotonin transporters, 5-HT1A, 5-HT2A, the noradrenaline transporter, MAO-B, mu-opioid, CB1), with a direction chip, the study's own magnitude ("6.6% per decade in caudate") and a source pill on every row

18 human imaging papers were added to the Europe PMC corpus; their 21 findings were each checked by an independent Opus judge, which rejected two (a CB1 rise with age seen only in women, and a cortical decline the tracer cannot attribute to D3)

The guided tour's highlight ring no longer points off-screen while the panel is still scrolling to the row it marks: a step that scrolls its target into view now waits for it to arrive (and finishes a stalled smooth scroll with a jump) before ringing it

A DailyMed label is now read with its route of administration, so a generic asenapine "tablet" counts as sublingual and "Extended Phenytoin Sodium Capsules" as extended release: their peak times now sit on the right formulation
Revex is listed as nalmefene's US injectable brand, not a French one

The citations downgraded in 3.114.0 are sourced again: amisulpride and lumateperone D2 antagonism (Stahl), asenapine and phenytoin peak times (US labels), Revex (Carlat), sibutramine's two metabolites on the serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine transporters, and disulfiram's active metabolite (Europe PMC abstracts)

A claim backed only by animal studies (rat, mouse, monkey...) now carries an "animal evidence" caution, naming the species, on drug bindings, metabolite bindings, projection transmitters and signs, and receptor regions

A judge verdict now belongs to the place a quote is cited, not to the quote alone, so a sentence reused to back a second claim is judged again for it: 341 citations were re-judged by an independent Opus judge, and the 8 it rejected were downgraded (two Tmax values, two D2 antagonist bindings, one brand, six sibutramine metabolite bindings)

Seven active metabolites (dehydroaripiprazole, M-II, desmethylselegiline, l-amphetamine, l-methamphetamine, desipramine from lofepramine, mCPP) now cite a sentence saying they are active, not just their half-life
The name-folding helpers used to join drug names across sources are now one shared function instead of several copies
Site-keyed judge stamps, split verdicts and the animal evidence flag are documented

Receptor panels gain a beta Downstream section: how activating the receptor changes the release of a transmitter, as a source describes the circuit. For example, H3 is an autoreceptor on presynaptic terminals whose activation decreases histamine release, and 5-HT2C sits on GABA interneurons and decreases dopamine release. Each line is its own sourced node

Drug panels gain a beta "Possible release changes via its bindings" section, derived from the drug's directional bindings: an antagonist reverses the effect of activation (pitolisant, an H3 antagonist, could increase histamine release), a binding with no known direction contributes nothing. It is computed, never stored, and worded conditionally

64 receptor release-modulation nodes over 25 receptors (17 autoreceptor, 47 heteroreceptor), from Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology and the receptors' Wikipedia articles, each quote checked on its page and confirmed by an independent Opus judge, which rejected two
The receptor-effect and release-modulation sourcing passes share one applier loop instead of two copies
The new node kind, its pipeline and its panels are documented

An active metabolite shared by several drugs is now defined once: nordazepam, for instance, is one record whichever of diazepam, clorazepate, prazepam or chlordiazepoxide makes it, so its bindings and half-life can never disagree between parents. The tally already counted each metabolite once by name, so the drug metabolite bindings figure is unchanged by this
The About panel lists metabolites.jsonl among the downloadable data files

Sibutramine is now marked as a prodrug: its two active metabolites, desmethylsibutramine and didesmethylsibutramine, each inhibit serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine reuptake, with their Ki read from the comparison table in sibutramine's Wikipedia article (15 to 49 nM). Six metabolite bindings are added and sibutramine's own three are removed
Brexpiprazole no longer lists DM-3411 as an active metabolite: its sources describe it as a major metabolite, not an active one
Three half-life quotes (cannabidiol, furosemide, bumetanide) point again at the sentence that states them, after their article text had shifted

Receptor and target panels gain an Effects section (beta): the clinical effects a source attributes to acting on that receptor in a given way, in humans, each with its own grade (for example H1 antagonism and sedation, D2 antagonism and prolactin elevation)

Drug panels gain a Possible effects via its bindings section (beta), derived rather than sourced for the drug: an effect appears only when the drug acts on a receptor in the same direction the source names, a bare affinity contributes nothing, and it is worded as something the drug could cause, not a side-effect list
66 receptor effects over 25 receptors and targets, quoted from Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology and the receptors' Wikipedia articles, each quote confirmed by an independent Opus judge

Ten more pathway transmitters and seven more pathway signs are now sourced, from research abstracts rather than textbooks (mostly rat, cat or mouse studies; the species is named on each). Among them: glutamate on the corticopontine, pontocerebellar, cerebellothalamic, perforant-path and mammillothalamic routes, accumbens-to-pallidum inhibition, and serotonin from the raphe to the olfactory bulb

Every projection group and every drug target is now sourced: the acetylcholine and noradrenaline groups from Nieuwenhuys, Kandel and Stahl, the NKCC1 cotransporter and the CGRP receptor from their Wikipedia articles

Written once for the section rather than copied onto 240 drugs, and deliberately unsourced, since the claim is about this dataset's coverage and no corpus could be cited for it.

Clomipramine now lists CYP2C19 among the enzymes that clear it. Adding the CPIC guidance in 3.93.0 showed the hole: the panel carried advice about this patient's CYP2C19 speed over an enzyme list that never mentioned CYP2C19. Nothing else here states the route (Stahl files the demethylation under CYP1A2, the English Wikipedia article names only CYP2D6, the US label names no enzyme at all), but CPIC does, in the sentence it writes for fast metabolizers: "Consider alternative drug not metabolized by CYP2C19; If clomipramine is warranted, utilize therapeutic drug monitoring". A drug panel now says what a clearance speed means for that prescription, in CPIC's own words: for each of the five metabolizer speeds, what to expect and what CPIC recommends doing about it, with the strength it attaches to that advice. It is not medical advice, and an ancestry is not a genotype: the frequency is how common a speed is in a group, never a reading of the patient in front of you.

CPIC's prescribing guidance joins the sources as corpus #15: 104 recommendation rows over 6 guidelines, every sentence quoted verbatim and re-derived from a committed export on every check, so none of it is a paraphrase. An enzyme with no clearance-speed chart now says so, and says why, instead of showing nothing where another enzyme shows a stacked bar. Three more drugs had a half-life on screen with no source behind it (alpidem, flupenthixol, dimenhydrinate); each now carries a quote a second model confirmed. A fourth, L-methylfolate, deliberately keeps its unsourced value: the only sentence the corpora state is about the d,l racemate, not the L form the drug is.

These release notes now appear as soon as you click "Start exploring", instead of waiting for the brain to finish assembling. They were also skipped entirely on any visit where that animation was cut short, such as grabbing the spread slider or following a link straight to a drug.

Nearly every pathway in the brain is drawn on both sides, but the books describe a tract once: the mirrored copy is our reading of the anatomy, not something any source states. The Projections section now says so at the top, as a single node with a red "no source" badge, rather than leaving the assumption unspoken behind some ninety arrows.

A metabolism row says two things: which liver enzyme clears the drug, and how much of the job it does (a major or minor route, a strong or weak effect). Only the first was ever checked against the source, so the second now has its own badge: 87 of the 147 rows that state a tier have a quote that really says it, and the other 60 read as unsourced. It matters because the drug-interaction rows are read through that tier: a major route meeting a strong inhibitor is the pair worth checking.

A pathway used to state three things under one badge: that it runs from A to B, what it carries, and whether it excites or inhibits. One sentence rarely says all three, so the transmitter and the sign are now separate facts with their own badges, and a source that only states the route no longer puts a green check on the rest. Of the 95 pathways, 56 have their transmitter attested and 9 of the 38 excitatory/inhibitory ones have their sign attested; the others read as unsourced, which is what they always were.
The data browser lists the two new fact types on their own, so you can read every pathway sign we cannot source in one list.

The US prescribing labels join the sources (DailyMed, the American drug-label archive), read for one fact: how long after a dose a drug peaks. It reaches the drugs the encyclopedia and the textbook never mention, and its labels are public documents anyone can open at the link on the source pill.
The time to peak is now sourced for 136 drugs instead of 90, so that many more see their simulated curve rise at their own pace rather than at the assumed two hours.

Four label sentences were claimed and then rejected by a second model, each for the same reason: a label often gives a peak for one tablet strength, one age group, one route or one moment, and none of those is the drug's general answer.

Drugs now carry a sourced time to peak: how long after a dose the blood concentration is at its highest. It sits beside the half-life in a new Timing section of the drug panel, with its own source pill, on the 90 drugs a corpus states it for.

The simulation's plasma curve rises at each drug's own pace instead of a single assumed two hours for everyone. A drug that peaks in half an hour and one that peaks in eight now look different, and the warnings box says which of the two a given curve is drawn from.

The time-to-peak pass read both stored corpora, claimed 92 values and shipped 90: a second model rejected two of them, one sentence being about a combination product and the other about a breakdown product rather than the drug itself.

The simulation tab now opens by saying what it is for, in both directions: how much of each receptor a combination of drugs engages, and which combination would come close to a profile you describe. The simulation's list of what it does not know now says up front that it is not exhaustive, and gained the one omission that most often surprises: the brain's own dopamine or serotonin, which a drug competes with at every receptor and which is why a measured occupancy never matches a test-tube affinity.

In the simulation, a receptor's bar now wears its own neurotransmitter's colour, the same one its pathways wear in the 3D brain: glutamate red, GABA blue, serotonin teal. Where two drugs share a receptor, the stronger one keeps the full colour and the others step down in shade, so the bar says which transmitter is engaged at a glance while still naming each drug on hover.
The repository map and the tool reference describe how a receptor bar is coloured and the palette it reads from.

The Wikipedia binding tables now fill in 64 more binding directions, across 15 drugs: where the article lists a drug's affinities, it often names the direction in the column beside them. Bindings still missing a direction drop from 712 to 648, and the overall sourced figure rises from 83% to 84%.

A second sourcing pass for binding directions, reading the "Action" column of a drug's own Wikipedia affinity table rather than its prose. A copied cell cannot be the wrong sentence, so this one is read by code with no model in the loop, and only a wording the dataset already knows is accepted: anything ambiguous is reported and left alone.
The repository map and the tool reference describe the new table pass beside the prose one it complements.

A drug binding is now two claims, and each is graded on its own: that the drug binds the target (a measured affinity settles that) and in which direction it acts (agonist, antagonist, and so on), which only a written source can settle. Before, 767 bindings known only by their affinity counted as fully sourced; they now show a red "no source" mark on their direction, and the overall sourced figure drops from 95% to 83%, which is the honest number.

A new sourcing pass reads each drug's own Wikipedia article for a sentence that states the direction of a binding known only by its affinity, checks the sentence is really on the page, and has a second model confirm it supports the claim. It closed 55 of those bindings; the rest stay marked as missing because the article never says.

In the simulation's "find drugs" answer, a pick that pulls against what you asked for (it only compensates a drug you already listed overshooting the target) now says so, and the fit percentage states how many receptors it was judged over.
The repository map lists the new binding-direction node kind and the Wikipedia pass that sources it.

A new **Simulation (beta)** section: pick a few drugs, set how much of each, and see what the combination does. The CGRP receptor, the target the newest migraine drugs were built for. It lists the six brain regions where it is expressed, each confirmed against the Allen human brain atlas, with the relative amount in each.
Molecule drawings for five drugs that had none: heroin, pentazocine, pethidine, rimonabant and tapentadol.

The six missing Parkinson's drugs: levodopa, carbidopa, benserazide, entacapone, tolcapone and istradefylline. This was the emptiest family the drug roster had left (3 of 9 present), and every new binding comes with its source quote.

Four antiepileptics: vigabatrin, ethosuximide, lacosamide and brivaracetam, in a new Anticonvulsant class. Vigabatrin brought a new target with it, GABA transaminase, the enzyme that breaks GABA down, so blocking it raises GABA everywhere at once (3e62c3c).

An affinity measured at or past 10 micromolar now reads as "tested, essentially inactive" whatever database it came from, instead of only in the one where that rule was already applied. Vigabatrin showed why: it inhibits its enzyme irreversibly, so the very weak number its assay reports is not a binding strength (ef9b52a).

Five general anesthetics: propofol, sevoflurane, isoflurane, etomidate and xenon, in a new Anesthetic class. They act on receptors the dataset already carried (GABA-A, NMDA, glycine, 5-HT3), so their absence said more about where the drug list came from than about the brain (d7c62ff).

Four drug panels showed a Wikipedia icon where the molecule belongs: rubidium chloride displayed a hazard diamond, nitrous oxide and calcium carbimide a category arrow, xenon the featured-article star. A substance whose article draws no structure now simply shows no image (e9277bd).

Seven psychedelics and dissociatives join the roster: psilocybin, mescaline, 2C-B, salvinorin A, ibogaine, phencyclidine and nitrous oxide. Only DMT was here before, though LSD, MDMA, ketamine and cannabis already were. Ibogaine arrives showing its measured affinities and claiming no mechanism. Its own literature says it touches the opioid, sigma and NMDA systems without ever saying whether it turns them up or down, so its page says exactly that rather than guessing a direction from a number.

A breakdown product of a drug has no page of its own, so looking one up opens the drug it comes from. Four medicines against nausea, vertigo and motion sickness join the roster: metoclopramide, granisetron, meclizine and dimenhydrinate. A medicine that is a chemical pairing of two others can now say so under its own name. Dimenhydrinate, the motion-sickness pill, is diphenhydramine bonded to a mild stimulant, so its panel points at both rather than claiming measurements that belong to another molecule.

A stray control character from the source extraction was sitting inside one brand name (Nuedexta) and inside the quote backing it. Removed, and the extractor now discards them.

Both affinity databases were read by a name match that ignored stereochemistry, so a single mirror-image form of a molecule was silently counted as the everyday form. Ketanserin was published as a sub-nanomolar 5-HT1F ligand on the strength of one measurement, while some forty others put the same drug a thousand to ten thousand times weaker across that whole receptor family, one of them on the very same receptor.
